title: Language Workshop
description: Fix typical German-speaker mistakes, upgrade your register, paraphrase, link ideas and master C1 sentence transformations.
intro: Accuracy and range are a big part of any speaking assessment. This workshop targets the mistakes German speakers make most often and the structures that make you sound like a C1 speaker – all with topic vocabulary on communication and media.

exercises.title: Typical grammar traps
exercises.instruction: Each sentence contains ONE mistake that German speakers often make. Tap the word(s) you think are wrong, then check the correction and explanation.

items.sentence: I live in Graz since 2020, so I know the local news well.
items.correction: I have lived in Graz since 2020, so I know the local news well.
items.explanation: With “since” + a point in time, English uses the present perfect (have lived), not the present simple. German “Ich wohne seit …” uses the present tense, which causes this mistake.

items.sentence: Can you give me some informations about the workshop?
items.correction: Can you give me some information about the workshop?
items.explanation: “Information” is uncountable in English: no plural -s. Say “some information” or “a piece of information”. The same applies to advice, news, evidence and feedback.

items.sentence: I want that you check this source before you share it.
items.correction: I want you to check this source before you share it.
items.explanation: English uses want + object + to-infinitive. “I want that …” is a direct translation of German “Ich will, dass …”.

items.sentence: The news are really depressing today.
items.correction: The news is really depressing today.
items.explanation: “News” looks plural but is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb.

items.sentence: He said me that the video was fake.
items.correction: He told me that the video was fake.
items.explanation: “Say” does not take a personal object directly. Use “tell someone” or “say to someone”.

items.sentence: I am agree with your point about privacy.
items.correction: I agree with your point about privacy.
items.explanation: “Agree” is a verb in English, not an adjective. No “am”.

items.sentence: We discussed about the advantages of AI in class.
items.correction: We discussed the advantages of AI in class.
items.explanation: “Discuss” takes a direct object – no “about”. (But: “We talked about …” / “a discussion about …”.)

items.sentence: If I would have known about the risks, I wouldn’t have posted it.
items.correction: If I had known about the risks, I wouldn’t have posted it.
items.explanation: In the if-clause of the third conditional, use the past perfect (had known), not “would have”.

exercises.title: False friends and word choice
exercises.instruction: Each sentence contains one word that is a typical German–English “false friend” or wrong word choice. Tap it, then compare your idea with the correction.

items.sentence: She made a photo of the protest and posted it immediately.
items.correction: She took a photo of the protest and posted it immediately.
items.explanation: In English you “take” a photo (German: ein Foto machen).

items.sentence: I’m going to become a new phone for my birthday.
items.correction: I’m going to get a new phone for my birthday.
items.explanation: “Become” means “werden”. German “bekommen” = get / receive.

items.sentence: I read the news every morning to stay actual.
items.correction: I read the news every morning to stay up to date.
items.explanation: “Actual” means “tatsächlich”. German “aktuell” = current / up to date.

items.sentence: My new classmate is really sympathetic – everyone likes him.
items.correction: My new classmate is really likeable – everyone likes him.
items.explanation: “Sympathetic” means “mitfühlend / verständnisvoll”. German “sympathisch” = likeable / nice / pleasant.

items.sentence: We could eventually meet tomorrow if you have time.
items.correction: We could possibly meet tomorrow if you have time.
items.explanation: “Eventually” means “schließlich / letztendlich”. German “eventuell” = possibly / perhaps.

items.sentence: I’ll control my emails after the meeting.
items.correction: I’ll check my emails after the meeting.
items.explanation: “Control” means “steuern / beherrschen”. German “kontrollieren” in this sense = check.

items.sentence: This website looks very serious, so you can probably trust it.
items.correction: This website looks very reputable, so you can probably trust it.
items.explanation: German “seriös” = reputable / trustworthy / respectable. “Serious” means “ernst”.

items.sentence: Most teenagers would rather lose their wallet than their handy.
items.correction: Most teenagers would rather lose their wallet than their mobile phone.
items.explanation: “Handy” is a German pseudo-anglicism. In English: mobile phone (BrE), cell phone (AmE) or smartphone. “Handy” in English means “useful”.

items.sentence: Whoever invented this fake story clearly has a lot of fantasy.
items.correction: Whoever invented this fake story clearly has a lot of imagination.
items.explanation: German “Fantasie (haben)” = imagination. “Fantasy” in English usually means a dream or a genre of fiction.

exercises.title: Preposition problems
exercises.instruction: Find the wrong preposition (or phrase) in each sentence. Tap it, then check the correction.

items.sentence: I found the article in the internet.
items.correction: I found the article on the internet.
items.explanation: English says “on the internet”, “on social media”, “on a website” (German: im Internet).

items.sentence: On the picture, we can see a family at dinner.
items.correction: In the picture, we can see a family at dinner.
items.explanation: Things are “in a picture / photo” (German: auf dem Bild). This one is very common in exam picture descriptions!

items.sentence: According to me, social media has more advantages than disadvantages.
items.correction: In my opinion, social media has more advantages than disadvantages.
items.explanation: “According to” refers to other people or sources: “according to the study”. For your own view, say “in my opinion / in my view”.

items.sentence: Many young people are afraid from missing out.
items.correction: Many young people are afraid of missing out.
items.explanation: afraid of (German: Angst vor).

items.sentence: Platforms should be responsible of the content they recommend.
items.correction: Platforms should be responsible for the content they recommend.
items.explanation: responsible for (German: verantwortlich für).

items.sentence: The report focuses to the effects of screen time.
items.correction: The report focuses on the effects of screen time.
items.explanation: focus on (German: sich konzentrieren auf).

items.sentence: A good monologue consists from three main parts.
items.correction: A good monologue consists of three main parts.
items.explanation: consist of (German: bestehen aus).

items.sentence: Students should participate on discussions about school rules.
items.correction: Students should participate in discussions about school rules.
items.explanation: participate in / take part in (German: teilnehmen an).

exercises.title: Register upgrade: from chat to exam
exercises.instruction: Rewrite each informal sentence in a formal, exam-appropriate style. Then compare your version with the model and check the key points. Many good answers are possible.

items.original: Loads of kids are on their phones all the time.
items.model_answer: A large number of young people spend a considerable amount of time on their smartphones.
key_points: loads of → a large number of / many
all the time → constantly / a considerable amount of time

items.original: Fake news is a really big problem and stuff.
items.model_answer: Misinformation is a serious problem with far-reaching consequences.

items.original: Social media’s kind of bad for you if you use it too much.
items.model_answer: Excessive use of social media may have negative effects on users’ wellbeing.
key_points: use it too much → excessive use (nominalisation)
bad for you → negative effects on wellbeing

items.original: Companies grab our data and make tons of money.
items.model_answer: Companies collect users’ personal data and profit considerably from it.

items.original: I think the government should do something about it.
items.model_answer: In my view, the government ought to take decisive action to address this issue.
key_points: I think → In my view / I would argue that
do something → take action / address the issue

items.original: Lots of people don’t get how algorithms work.
items.model_answer: Many people lack a clear understanding of how algorithms function.
key_points: don’t get → lack an understanding of / do not understand

exercises.title: Paraphrasing without repeating
exercises.instruction: Paraphrase each sentence so that it keeps the same meaning but uses different key words and/or structures. Paraphrasing helps when you summarise a stimulus text in the exam.

items.original: Many teenagers spend several hours a day on social media.
items.model_answer: It is common for young people to devote a few hours daily to social platforms.
key_points: change of structure (It is common for …)

items.original: Fact-checkers check whether claims are true.
items.model_answer: Fact-checkers verify the accuracy of statements.
key_points: whether … true → the accuracy / truthfulness of

items.original: The law protects people’s personal data.
items.model_answer: The legislation safeguards individuals’ private information.

items.original: Influencers must say when a post is an advert.
items.model_answer: Creators are required to disclose sponsored content.

items.original: Deepfakes make it harder to trust videos.
items.model_answer: Synthetic media undermines confidence in video evidence.
key_points: make it harder to trust → undermine confidence / erode trust

exercises.title: Linking words: meaning and grammar
exercises.instruction: Choose the linking word that fits both the MEANING and the GRAMMAR of the sentence. Read the explanations – many mistakes come from confusing despite/although or whereas/however.

questions.prompt: ___ the evidence is mixed, many schools have banned phones.
questions.explanation: “Although” + clause (subject + verb). “Despite” needs a noun or -ing form; “however” starts a new sentence.

questions.prompt: ___ the risks, many parents give their children smartphones at a young age.
questions.explanation: “Despite” + noun phrase (the risks). “Although / even though” would need a clause: “Although there are risks, …”.

questions.prompt: Platforms earn money from our attention. ___, they have little incentive to reduce screen time.
questions.explanation: The second sentence is a result of the first, so “consequently” (= as a result) fits.

questions.prompt: Print sales are falling, ___ digital subscriptions are growing at some newspapers.
questions.explanation: “Whereas” contrasts two facts within one sentence.

questions.prompt: Labels on AI content are helpful. ___, they cannot replace critical thinking.
questions.explanation: “Nevertheless” (= however, despite this) introduces a contrast.

questions.prompt: Many apps use dark patterns. ___, some make it very difficult to cancel a subscription.
questions.explanation: The second sentence gives an example of dark patterns.

questions.prompt: Users cannot avoid personalised ads ___ they change their settings manually.
questions.explanation: “Unless” = except if. The only way to avoid the ads is to change the settings.

questions.prompt: ___ deepfakes becoming more realistic, detection is getting harder.
questions.explanation: “With + noun + -ing” expresses a cause or accompanying situation. “Although” and “because” need a full clause (“because deepfakes are becoming …”), and “despite” has the wrong meaning.

exercises.title: Linking words by function
exercises.instruction: Sort the linking words by their function. Knowing the function helps you avoid using the wrong connector in your monologue.
exercises.explanation: Vary your connectors: instead of repeating “and”, “but” and “so”, use furthermore, nevertheless and consequently. But don’t overload your speech with them – one per idea is enough.

exercises.title: Build a cohesive paragraph
exercises.instruction: Put the sentences in the correct order to form a logical paragraph. Use the linking words and reference words (this, however, in turn) as clues.
items: Personalised feeds are designed to show us content we are likely to engage with.
At first glance, this seems convenient: we see more of what we like.
However, this convenience may come at a price.
If we are mainly shown views that match our own, we may start to believe that everyone thinks like us.
This, in turn, could make it harder to understand people who disagree with us.
For this reason, it is worth deliberately seeking out sources with different perspectives.
exercises.explanation: Clues: “this seems convenient” refers back to sentence 1; “However, this convenience” picks up “convenient”; “This, in turn” refers to the belief in sentence 4; “For this reason” introduces the conclusion. Reference words create cohesion – use them in your speaking too.

exercises.title: Structure a monologue
exercises.instruction: These are the parts of a strong exam monologue about a picture. Put them in the most logical order.
items: Today I’d like to talk about a picture that shows a family at dinner, all looking at their phones.
In the foreground, two teenagers are scrolling, while their parents are checking messages too.
This scene suggests that digital devices can make us “together alone”.
On the one hand, phones can push families apart because real conversations become rarer.
On the other hand, family group chats and video calls help many families stay in touch.
Personally, I believe the device is not the problem – it is how and when we use it.
To sum up, phone-free meals could be a simple way to bring families back to the table.
exercises.explanation: Introduction → description → interpretation → arguments on both sides → personal opinion → conclusion. This clear structure is easy for the examiner to follow and works for almost any topic.

exercises.title: Key word transformations I
exercises.instruction: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first. Use the word given and do not change it. Use between two and five words, including the word given.

items.original: People say that the video was created with AI.
items.explanation: Passive reporting structure: subject + is said + to have been (past).

items.original: I regret sharing that post.
items.explanation: wish + past perfect for regrets about the past.

items.original: It wasn’t necessary for you to delete your account, but you did.
items.explanation: needn’t have + past participle = you did it, but it was unnecessary. (“Didn’t need to delete” does not make clear that you actually did it.)

items.original: They will probably introduce stricter rules next year.
items.explanation: be likely to + passive infinitive (to be introduced).

items.original: It’s possible that the account was hacked.
items.explanation: might have been + past participle = speculation about the past (passive).

items.original: Despite having been warned, he posted the photo.
items.gapped: He posted the photo ___ been warned.
items.explanation: even though + clause (he had been warned).

exercises.title: Key word transformations II: inversion and more
exercises.instruction: Extra challenge. Complete the second sentence using the word given, so that it has a similar meaning. Use between two and five words, including the word given.

items.original: As soon as the video was posted, it went viral.
items.gapped: No ___ posted than it went viral.
items.explanation: No sooner + past perfect with inversion (had the video been) + than.

items.original: The company didn’t apologise until the scandal became public.
items.gapped: ___ the scandal became public did the company apologise.
items.explanation: Only when/after + clause, followed by inversion in the main clause (did the company apologise).

items.original: I’d prefer you not to post photos of me.
items.explanation: would rather + subject + past simple to express a preference about someone else’s action.

items.original: The influencer had just posted the ad when the complaints started.
items.gapped: ___ the ad when the complaints started.
items.explanation: Hardly + inversion (had + subject + past participle) + when.

items.original: People believe that the leak came from inside the company.
items.gapped: The leak ___ from inside the company.
items.explanation: Passive reporting structure with a perfect infinitive for a past event.

items.original: Nobody told me that the post was sponsored.
items.gapped: I ___ that the post was sponsored.
items.explanation: Passive: Nobody told me → I was not informed.

exercises.title: Sound like C1: emphasis and nominalisation
exercises.instruction: Rewrite each sentence using the structure given in brackets. These structures add emphasis and sophistication. Compare your answer with the model.

items.original: Algorithms worry me most. (cleft sentence: What …)
items.model_answer: What worries me most is the power of algorithms.
key_points: puts emphasis on the last part

items.original: People rarely check their sources. (inversion: Rarely …)
items.model_answer: Rarely do people check their sources.

items.original: Because platforms are not transparent, users don’t trust them. (nominalisation: The lack of …)
items.model_answer: The lack of transparency on platforms leads to a loss of trust among users.

items.original: We should teach students to use technology. We should also teach them to question it. (Not only …)
items.model_answer: Not only should we teach students to use technology, but we should also teach them to question it.
key_points: but … also in the second part

items.original: The government didn’t act until a scandal happened. (It was not until …)
items.model_answer: It was not until a scandal broke that the government took action.
key_points: It was not until + time/event + that + clause
“a scandal broke” is a natural collocation
